name: Cogent Communications, Inc.

profile.reading: This is a Cogent Communications data center in Phoenix, Arizona, part of Cogent Communications Holdings network, though no source checked this session disclosed a specific street address, power capacity, or square footage for this particular Phoenix building, an honest gap this registry records rather than estimates. Cogent Communications was founded in 1999 by David Schaeffer, who remains chief executive, launching at the height of the dot-com era with backing from angel investors including members of Keiretsu Forum, and is headquartered in Washington, D.C. Within its first three years the company pursued an aggressive acquisition strategy, reportedly acquiring 13 failing telecommunications carriers and purchasing about 14 billion dollars in capital assets, including roughly 4 billion dollars in property, plant, and equipment, for a combined 60 million dollars between 2001 and 2004, including the major United States assets of PSINet and the LambdaNet operations in France and Spain. Cogent operates a large scale internet backbone network carrying more than 100 terabits per second of traffic under its own Autonomous System Number 174, reported about 1,947 employees and 940.9 million dollars in revenue as of 2023, and offers colocation services within data centers as part of its broader network and hosting business, of which this Phoenix facility is one location.
profile.research_note: Cogent's own site confirms the Phoenix office/PoP address (3410 E. University Dr Suite 350, Phoenix AZ 85034) but Cogent does not publish IT capacity, sqft, or certification figures for its network PoP/colocation sites.

reading:
Cogent Communications Holdings is a publicly traded internet backbone operator listed on NASDAQ as CCOI and filing with the SEC under CIK 0001158324, headquartered in Washington, D.C. Its business is IP transit and wavelength services over its own fibre network, and it is in this registry because that network needs buildings. Cogent's data centres are network sites first. They terminate its fibre, house its routers, and sell colocation mainly to customers who want to sit next to Cogent's transit rather than to tenants shopping for wholesale space. That is a different business from the wholesale developers elsewhere in this registry, and it explains the scale of the sites.

The registry's Arizona row is Cogent's Phoenix facility at 3410 East University Drive. Cogent's own page describes 5,914 square feet of data centre space with 42U cabinets and private cages, card controlled access around the clock, camera surveillance, HVAC, fire detection and suppression, uninterruptible power with generator backup, ports up to 400 gigabit Ethernet and wave services. Cogent publishes no megawatt figure for the site.

That absence needs a correction on the record, because a capacity figure of roughly 12 megawatts for Cogent Phoenix has circulated through third party directories and has been repeated as though it were a site specification. It cannot be reconciled with what Cogent publishes. A room of 5,914 square feet at 12 megawatts would sit above 2,000 watts per square foot, far outside anything a carrier point of presence of that vintage is built for. Cogent's own disclosures around its network acquisitions point the same way. Before buying the Sprint wireline business from T-Mobile, Cogent described operating 55 facilities with 70 megawatts of power between them, roughly 1.3 megawatts a site on average. This registry therefore records no capacity for Cogent Phoenix rather than carrying a number the operator does not publish and that its own footprint contradicts.

The wireline acquisition is the larger story for Cogent as a data centre operator and worth noting here even though it does not touch the Arizona row directly. The deal brought Cogent 482 technical buildings held outright, about 1.6 million square feet in total. Cogent identified the largest 45 of those switch sites, roughly 1.3 million square feet carrying about 160 megawatts of already installed power, as candidates to convert into colocation data centres, and has been working through that conversion since 2023, later selling a batch of former Sprint wireline data centres to an infrastructure buyer as part of a deleveraging push. The installed power in those legacy telephone switch buildings, put in decades ago for equipment that drew far more than modern routers, is the asset Cogent is monetising, and it is utility service and rectifier plant rather than critical IT load. As an SEC filer Cogent's corporate financials are fully documented, but its filings report network and financial metrics rather than facility specifications, so site level figures for individual buildings such as Phoenix remain sparse in the primary record.
